body_markdown:
Few folks have the wherewithal to construct a vehicle saluting the P-40 Warhawk, one of WWII’s most memorable aircraft. James Trudeau, 74, of Punta Gorda, Florida, is clearly not your average tinkerer. In 1986, after this Hagerty member was injured as a police officer, he switched to restoring and test-flying aircraft as his day job and took up car construction as his hobby.


Courtesy James Trudeau


*Welcome to **Homegrown** —a series about homebuilt cars and the ingenuity of their visionary creators. Know a car and builder that might fit the bill? Send us an email at[tips@hagerty.com](https://www.hagerty.com/mailto:tips@hagerty.com) with the subject line HOMEGROWN.[Read about more Homegrown creations here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/homegrown/) . —Ed.*


Built by Curtiss-Wright in Buffalo, New York, the P-40 fighter-bomber flew all over the world in the hands of two dozen nations. Powered by a supercharged Allison V-12 producing over 1000 horsepower, the P-40 had a top speed of 350 mph and a ceiling topping 29,000 feet. Its most distinctive touch was a shark maw painted on the chin scoop feeding air to the engine’s radiator and oil cooler. Six machine guns were packed into the wings, and by the end of its service life up to 2000 lbs of bombs could be carried on the aircraft’s bottom hardpoints.


While nearly 14,000 P-40s were built during WWII, only 28 remain airworthy today (not counting Trudeau’s wingless tribute).


A Curtiss P-40E Warhawk airborne near Chino, California.


Scott Germain/Stocktrek Images


Explaining how he acquired the skills needed to build what he calls his rat rod, Trudeau notes, “At 5 years of age I began tearing things apart at my father’s marina. After fourth grade, dad sent me to Mercury Marine’s training school in Warwick, Rhode Island. My final exam was assembling a 100-horse outboard motor’s power head. Mine ran perfectly, earning me a marine mechanic’s certificate…at 10 years of age.


“Back home, I learned woodworking and auto body repair skills. I joined the Navy in 1970 but, following boot camp, I was discharged because I’m color blind. I then joined the local police force where I served as a law enforcement officer for 14 years while also working at a local airport. After building my own hangar, I taught myself metal shaping, machining, welding, fiberglass repair, and how to fly—the essential skills for restoring aircraft.


“My first aviation business in Ware, Massachusetts, was rebuilding planes and refurbishing interiors. Over 30 years, my employees and I refinished some 800 planes, many hot rods, and countless car interiors. Then in 2000, I relocated to Florida to establish a warbird maintenance and restoration business with a focus on T-28 (Navy) aircraft.


A T-28 that Trudeau restored for a client.


Courtesy James Trudeau


“My wife Janet suggested we create something from the huge inventory of T-28 parts we had lying around. Since I never liked cookie-cutter hot rods, that struck me as a brilliant idea!


“I started building my road-going, half-size P-40 in 2008. Construction took about two years. All the sheet metal is T-28, reformed to match the P-40’s silhouette. My canopy is a cut-down T-28 component and the electrical panel also came from a T-28. Interestingly, my repurposed airspeed indicator provides an accurate mph reading. What was originally the T-28’s control lever for adjusting fuel mixture and propeller pitch works nicely as my gear shifter. My cockpit is equipped with two tandem bucket seats from a T-28 with parachutes serving as cushions.


Courtesy James Trudeau


Courtesy James Trudeau


Courtesy James Trudeau


“I built a frame out of 7071-T6 2×4-inch aluminum tubing. To keep it out of sight, this backbone is located about halfway up and into the fuselage. I fabricated a rigid front axle equipped with coil-over dampers. The rear axle has air springs inflated by a B-17 compressor with a controller from a 50-caliber machine gun.


“My powertrain came from a ‘72 Chevy Suburban; a 454 cubic inch V-8 and a Turbo-Hydramatic transmission spin the differential. My radiator is a $50 surplus component originally intended for excavator use. A fuel tank located behind the cockpit carries 17.5 gallons of gas. All my exterior ductwork is functional.


Courtesy James Trudeau


“Since we reside in Florida, air conditioning is essential. The big block V-8 located just ahead of the cockpit serves nicely as our audio system. I fabricated new exhaust manifolds to help this engine resemble a V-12.


“Nervous about obtaining license plates, I very carefully installed the mandatory lights and safety gear. Remarkably, all the DMV inspector really wanted was photos of this car. Once those were obtained, he declared, ‘Go forth, it’s a show car!’


Courtesy James Trudeau


Courtesy James Trudeau


Courtesy James Trudeau


Courtesy James Trudeau


Courtesy James Trudeau


“My most unusual feature is steering via an aircraft stick instead of a car wheel. Seventy degrees of movement through an elliptical sprocket provides the equivalent of 3.5 turns lock-to-lock needed to guide the front wheels. This arrangement is a bit touchy in curves, but it does hold my car true on straight roads.


Courtesy James Trudeau


“Because my concoction weighs only 1900 pounds and will burn rubber in any gear, it’s a blast to drive! One issue is watching out for the rubberneckers who have a habit of steering towards my motor marvel.


Courtesy James Trudeau


Courtesy James Trudeau


Courtesy James Trudeau


“I’ve driven this counterfeit P-40 about a thousand miles to attend a dozen or so shows where it always drew a crowd. The highest speed I’ve seen is around 100 mph. In 2017,[I was invited to participate in the Turkey Rod Run at Daytona Beach.](https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=547420752395836)


“Four years ago, a gentleman from Belgium made me an offer I couldn’t refuse to buy my car: 20 times more than my parts investment. Reluctantly, I let my creation go to attend to two other cars in my collection: a 2014 Fiat 500 repowered with a Mercury Marine four-cylinder engine and a 1955 Bonneville belly tanker. I’m also working on a 1939 Indy racer once owned by Barney Oldfield.”


Trudeau’s experience proves our adage: In the Homegrown lane, there’s always an interesting new project to commandeer any capable craftsman’s spare time.


Courtesy James Trudeau
